lesson.title: Learned DBMS components: predictions need a systems contract
lesson.short: Cardinality · plan ranking · learned indexes · robust evaluation
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: A model can reduce prediction error and still make a database slower. Follow the decision from features to plan to measured execution.
goals: Locate learning at cardinality estimation, cost/ranking, indexing and configuration boundaries.
Calculate q-error and end-to-end break-even cost.
Design a leakage-resistant evaluation with a safe conventional fallback.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
Study path. Use the selectivity and plan-choice ideas from lessons 17–18. Start with the arithmetic and paper exercise; model implementation is optional.

This original companion follows the supplied syllabus; it is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment. Activities and timings are practice guidance. Assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Four places to introduce learning
sections.html:
A database exposes several different prediction problems. A cardinality estimator predicts rows after a filter or join. A cost model or plan ranker helps choose among correct physical plans. A learned index predicts where a key is likely to be found in sorted data, then verifies/corrects the position. A configuration advisor selects knobs, indexes or resource allocations for a workload.

These components have different contracts. A wrong cardinality estimate normally hurts performance without changing SQL semantics. A learned index that skips verification can return the wrong key. A configuration choice can change memory pressure or concurrency for every query. Define input, output, fallback, update behavior and correctness checks before selecting a neural architecture.

For a learned sorted-array lookup, suppose a model predicts position 420, with a valid maximum error of 6 for the supported keys. Search and verify inside positions 414–426. If that bound is only measured on training keys, it does not establish correctness for arbitrary future keys. Inserts, deletes and distribution shifts require an updated bound, a correct search strategy or a fallback.

Key takeaway

A learned component is useful only inside a complete algorithm that preserves correctness and accounts for prediction, maintenance and fallback cost.

sections.title: Worked example: correlation and q-error
sections.html:
Original example. A table has 100,000 customers. Ten percent live in City A; five percent have a local commuter pass. Every pass holder lives in City A. Independence would estimate the conjunction as 100,000 × 0.10 × 0.05 = 500 rows; the actual result is 5,000.

For positive actual cardinality c and estimate ĉ, q-error is max(ĉ/c, c/ĉ). The independence estimate has q-error 10. An estimate of 4,000 has q-error 1.25. For zero cardinalities, explicitly document a convention such as replacing both values by max(value, 1); never mix conventions silently.

Better q-error is not automatically a better plan. Errors at a small, unimportant subplan may matter less than a threshold error that makes a hash table spill. Record both estimation quality and the downstream execution plan, memory usage and runtime.

Exercise: an estimate is 60,000 and the true count is 15,000. What is q-error?

Worked answer. 4. The estimate is four times too large. Q-error treats a fourfold under-estimate symmetrically, but a DBMS can pay very different costs for over- and under-estimation.

sections.title: Prediction quality versus end-to-end benefit
sections.html:
Original timing example. A conventional optimizer takes 2 ms and chooses an 80 ms plan. A learned selector takes 9 ms and chooses a 60 ms plan. End-to-end totals are 82 ms and 69 ms: speedup is 82/69 ≈ 1.19, not 80/60 ≈ 1.33. For a short query with 3 ms conventional execution and 2 ms learned execution, totals become 5 ms versus 11 ms. The same inference overhead reverses the outcome.

Suppose training and label collection cost 1,800 seconds and deployment saves 13 ms per request. The simplified break-even volume is 1,800/0.013 ≈ 138,462 requests, before retraining and operational overhead. Report training cost separately and show a stated amortization scenario.

Useful measurements include total workload time, per-query speedup distribution, planning latency, timeout count and catastrophic regressions. Include a native optimizer, a simple heuristic and a candidate-plan oracle: the fastest measured plan among the same supplied candidates. It uses hindsight, so it is an evaluation reference rather than a deployable selector. Comparing the learned choice with this oracle separates failure to rank available plans from failure to propose a good plan.

Exercise: the candidate-plan oracle takes 40 ms, the learned choice takes 60 ms, and the native plan takes 100 ms. What does each gap diagnose?

Worked answer. The 20 ms gap between learned and candidate oracle suggests ranking opportunity. The oracle is not the globally optimal plan: missing candidates may leave further opportunity. The 40 ms native-to-learned difference measures execution savings only; add planning and collection overhead for an end-to-end claim.

sections.title: Read recent research as testable claims
sections.html:
Lehmann, Sulimov and Stockinger (PVLDB 2024) audit the whole learned-query-optimizer pipeline. Their experiments show that train/test design can change conclusions, and the native PostgreSQL optimizer wins most of their tested comparisons. Read this as a warning about evaluation scope, rather than proof that all learning is ineffective.

GRASP (PVLDB 2025) addresses a different contract: learn cardinalities from queries and observed counts without raw-table access. A query template is a query’s structure with changing literal values replaced by placeholders; its join pattern is part of that structure. GRASP’s compositional design targets unseen or imbalanced join templates and range-predicate distribution shifts. Check which SQL fragments it supports and how it handles data updates before transferring the result to a new DBMS.

Theory bridge. Join Size Bounds using Lp-Norms on Degree Sequences (PODS 2024) studies upper bounds rather than predictions. A one-sided bound can serve a different purpose from a highly accurate average estimate. The linked manuscript began in 2023; its PODS 2024 acceptance is verified in the conference list.

Mathematical bridge: a bound rather than a prediction. Join R(k) with S(k). For keys k1 and k2, R contains 3 and 1 rows; S contains 2 and 2 rows. Thus a=(3,1) and b=(2,2) are aligned vectors of row counts for the same keys. Key k1 contributes 3×2=6 matching pairs and k2 contributes 1×2=2, so the output has 3×2+1×2=8 rows. The Cauchy–Schwarz upper bound is √(3²+1²) × √(2²+2²)=√80≈8.94, so the integer count is at most 8. A point predictor of 7 has small error but is not an upper bound. This two-vector exercise illustrates the distinction; it is not the paper’s general theorem.

sections.title: Paper-first experiment: generalization without leakage
sections.html:
For the query-template idea above, WHERE city = 'A' and WHERE city = 'B' share WHERE city = ?; adding AND pass = 1 changes the structure.

Paper-first task. All six queries count rows in the same fixed Customer snapshot:

QueryWHERE condition
Q1city = 'A'
Q2city = 'B'
Q3city = 'C'
Q4city = 'A' AND pass = 1
Q5city = 'B' AND pass = 1
Q6city = 'C' AND pass = 1
Group the templates. Propose a new-literal test and a new-template test. Which queries may tune the method?

Worked answer. Q1–Q3 share one template; Q4–Q6 share another. To test new literals on known templates, train on Q1/Q4, tune on validation queries Q2/Q5, and leave Q3/Q6 untouched for the final test. To test a new template instead, train on Q1, tune on Q2/Q3, and hold all of Q4–Q6 out. These are two alternative experiment designs. If Q4 influences tuning in the second design, its template is no longer unseen. A later workload period is a third test regime; fix the date boundary before inspecting its results.

Optional implementation. With basic SQL, train/validation/test splitting and a CPU regression tool, extend this to one table and a small fixed set of labeled queries. Deliver a split file, estimates/counts, a q-error table, a complete timing breakdown and one fallback test. Compare native estimates, a histogram or simple regression baseline, and the proposed method under the same label budget. Log query/template IDs, plans, dataset hash and random seed; include collection/training cost, timeouts and worst regressions.

An ablation repeats an experiment after removing or changing one component while keeping other conditions fixed. For example, halve the training labels while keeping the snapshot, model, split and timing protocol fixed. Then test representation and workload overlap separately. A confidence score does not establish correctness: unsupported SQL, unfamiliar input and inference failures need a conventional fallback. Begin on CPU; GPU training is an optional extension. A defensible negative result is a successful study.

Key takeaway

Evaluate the workload you want to generalize to, not just a convenient random split.

sections.title: Seminar exercise and answer
sections.html:
A paper reports median q-error 1.4 and a mean execution speedup of 2×. It excludes training, optimizer inference and three timed-out queries. Write a fair conclusion and three follow-up questions.

Reveal a defensible response

Worked answer. “The method improves the reported estimation metric and the selected execution-only comparison under the paper’s workload. End-to-end advantage and worst-case robustness remain unclear.” Ask for a timeout-aware workload total, complete planning/training costs and a template-held-out or time-held-out evaluation. Also inspect whether the baseline received comparable tuning and whether the same correctness checks were applied.

quiz.question: A learned selector saves 4 ms of execution but adds 7 ms of planning. What follows?
options: It improves end-to-end latency by 3 ms.
Q-error must be below one.
The query result must be incorrect.
It worsens end-to-end latency by 3 ms, before amortized training cost.
quiz.explanation: The execution saving is smaller than the added planning overhead; performance and SQL correctness are separate questions.

questions.question: An estimator predicts 500 rows when the actual positive count is 5,000. What is its q-error?
questions.explanation: Q-error is max(estimate/actual, actual/estimate), so max(0.1,10)=10.

questions.question: Why hold complete query templates out of a learned-optimizer test?
options: To avoid measuring query latency.
To test generalization beyond structurally similar training queries.
To ensure all cardinality estimates are exact.
To guarantee the new optimizer wins.
questions.explanation: A random query split can share near-identical structures across train and test. Template-held-out evaluation tests a different and often harder generalization contract.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A learned index predicts a position. What else is needed for correct lookup?
options: An embedding similarity score.
A verified search/correction procedure and an appropriate bound or fallback.
Only a low average training loss.
A GPU in every case.
questions.explanation: Average predictive accuracy does not guarantee that a specific key is found. The enclosing search algorithm must handle prediction error and updates correctly.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is the difference between a cardinality upper bound and a point estimate?
options: An upper bound must equal the exact count.
An upper bound is intended to never be below the true value under its assumptions; a point estimate need not satisfy that.
A point estimate is always more expensive.
They are identical if the estimate has low mean error.
questions.explanation: A one-sided mathematical guarantee has a different contract from typical prediction accuracy. Its assumptions must still hold.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

lqo.authors: Claude Lehmann, Pavel Sulimov, Kurt Stockinger
lqo.supports: An end-to-end learned-optimizer evaluation framework; sensitivity to training/test design; PostgreSQL wins in most tested comparisons, depending on split. This is evidence about the evaluated systems and protocol, not impossibility of learned optimization.
